Generalized Understanding: 1. GSBPM Overview and Purpose What is GSBPM?  The GSBPM defines and describes a standardized set of activities required for the production of official statistics within statistical organizations.  It provides a harmonized framework and common terminology to support modernization, process assessment, documentation, integration, and sharing of methods/components across statistical workflows.  Core Functions: Guides process documentation, software development, integration of metadata/quality frameworks, and enables assessment of statistical processes.  Used flexibly: can be applied as-is, adapted for organization-specific needs, or referenced during communication and modernization.  Target Audience: Producers of official statistics (national/international).  Users: policymakers, researchers, businesses, general public.  Stakeholders: also includes respondents, data suppliers/holders, and others impacted by statistical production.  2. Principles of GSBPM Operation Non-Sequential/Iterative: GSBPM phases and sub-processes are not strictly linear; activities may be repeated, looped, performed in parallel, or omitted, depending on context. Formal “sign-off” between phases/sub-processes may be organization-dependent.  Applicability: Covers survey, census, administrative, private, big data, geospatial, and other data sources. Also applies to processes for revising outputs or compiling national/international statistics.  Modularity: Organizations may aggregate phases (e.g., treat initial phases as a planning stage) or specify sub-processes in greater detail (“Tasks” level; see Annex).  Technical Neutrality: Processes remain valid regardless of technologies or methods used (AI, ML, APIs, etc.).  Version Changes: GSBPM evolves via international consensus, with updates focused on clarity, technology, new data sources, and alignment with other models.  3. GSBPM Hierarchical Structure Level 0: Statistical Business Process.  Level 1: Eight Phases (Specify Needs, Design, Build, Collect, Process, Analyse, Disseminate, Evaluate).  Level 2: Sub-processes within each phase (captured in your JSON).  Level 3 (Optional): Tasks—lower-level activities within sub-processes (see Annex I for external references and structure).  4. Overarching Activities These central activities span all phases of GSBPM and govern the conduct of statistical production: 4.1 Quality Management Controls and evaluates process/product quality throughout the lifecycle.  Relies on established frameworks (e.g. ISO 9000-2015), institutional policies, and continuous feedback loops ('Plan–Run–Evaluate–Improve').  Involves risk assessment, quality criteria/targets, user feedback, auditing, and review of quality indicators (see recommended indicators at UNECE link).  4.2 Metadata Management Ensures creation, linkage, maintenance, and archiving of metadata alongside data at every process stage.  Operational management is distinct from corporate-level (GAMSO) concerns.  GSIM supports consistent metadata handling.  4.3 Data Management Covers planning, security, custody, quality, archiving, retention, and disposal of statistical data.  Aligns with lifecycle principles and compliance requirements.  4.4 Process Data Management Systematizes and uses process data (paradata, execution logs, fieldwork info) to optimize efficiency, troubleshoot, and feed into process improvement and quality assessment.  4.5 Knowledge Management Maintains up-to-date documentation (manuals, guides, lessons learned), enabling repeatability, training, and continuous improvement.  4.6 Data Supplier Management Engages and profiles data suppliers, manages burden, contacts, agreements, and technical support.  Includes cross-process engagement for register management, solving operational issues, and responding to unexpected data changes.  5. GAMSO (Generic Activity Model for Statistical Organisations): Provides corporate/strategic activity context, encompassing areas not directly related to statistical production.  GSBPM is 'nested' within GAMSO’s 'production' activity area.  Organization-wide activities (e.g., HR, strategic quality management) are handled in GAMSO.  GSIM (Generic Statistical Information Model): Reference framework for defining, managing, and exchanging statistical information (data and metadata).  GSIM classes serve as standardized inputs/outputs for GSBPM sub-processes, improving interoperability and metadata-driven systems.  6. GSBPM Entities and Terminology . GSBPM Entities and Terminology Stakeholder Definitions: Users: End-consumers of statistical outputs.  Respondents: Data providers for primary collection.  Data Holders: Custodians of (often non-statistical) datasets; may supply data.  Data Suppliers: Data holders that provide data to NSOs/statistical organizations.  Stakeholders: Inclusive category for all above plus others affected/involved.  7. Other Uses and Practical Applications Documentation Structure: Framework for organizing process documentation, training materials, best practices.  Method/Software Sharing: Enables efficient share/reuse of statistical methods/components across organizations.  Quality Assessment: Provides foundation for process-based quality benchmarking, integration of metadata/quality work.  Cost/Performance Measurement: Basis for operational cost tracking, performance review, gap analysis, and modernization targeting.  Capacity Building: Supports structured technical knowledge and process skills.  External Harmonization: Tool for aligning terminology and business processes with external data suppliers (administrative, geospatial data).  Education/Training: Underpins curriculum and skills description for statistical production roles.  8. Change Log and Version Principles GSBPM Versioning: Major revisions occur only with strong business cases and broad consensus due to global adoption.  Recent Updates (v5.2): Emphasize data sources beyond surveys, non-sequential flows, administrative/geospatial data, modernized terminology, role of ML/AI, process security, and overarching activities.  No structural changes in phases/sub-processes between recent versions; naming/clarity improvements made.  9. Concrete software/tool recommendations, as these are technology-neutral in GSBPM.  11. Summary Guidance for the AI Assistant When evaluating future updates, focus on: Changes to overarching activities (especially Quality, Metadata, Data, and Supplier Management); Added/removed/renamed phases, sub-processes, or tasks; Shifts in applicability, entities, or recommended practices, especially for new data sources/technologies; Alterations in relationships to GAMSO, GSIM, or external standards/frameworks; Novel operational guidance or process formalization.  Retain awareness that GSBPM is a flexible, broad, harmonizing model—local adaptations and future changes are expected to respect this principle.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This phase is triggered when a need for new statistics is identified, perhaps resulting from user feedback, or a review is undertaken. It includes all activities associated with engaging stakeholders to identify their detailed statistical needs (current or future), proposing high level solution options and preparing a business case, which may weigh the benefits of addressing these needs against expected costs, risks and other requirements, considering the public good arising from meeting those needs and the implications for respondents, users and other stakeholders. The Specify Needs phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 7), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.

The human role is thereby focused on creative, interpretive, or complex tasks—like defining strategic priorities, balancing trade-offs, and making final judgments. Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process includes the initial investigation and identification of what statistics are needed and what is needed of the statistics. It may be triggered by a new information request from users, an environmental change such as a reduced budget, a periodic review, or respondent feedback. Action plans from evaluations of previous iterations of the production cycle (including from respondent feedback) or from other programmes might provide an input to this sub-process. It also includes consideration of practice amongst other (national and international) statistical organisations producing similar data and the methods used by those organisations.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process focuses on consulting with the internal and external stakeholders and confirming in detail the needs for the statistics. A good understanding of user needs is required so that the statistical organisation knows not only what it is expected to deliver, but also when, how, and perhaps most importantly, why. For the second and subsequent iterations of this sub-process, the main focus will be on determining whether previously identified needs have changed. This detailed understanding of user needs is the critical part of this sub-process.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process checks whether current sources of data could meet user requirements and the conditions under which they would be available, including any restrictions on their use. An assessment of possible alternatives would normally include research into potential administrative or other non-statistical sources of data (e.g. privately-held data or “Big Data”), to: Determine whether they would be suitable for use for statistical purposes (e.g. the extent to which administrative concepts match data requirements, and whether the timeliness and quality of the data, security, and continuity of data supply are suitable); Assess the division of responsibilities between data suppliers and the statistical organisation; Check necessary ICT resources (e.g. data storage, technology required to handle incoming data and data processing) as well as any provision agreements with data suppliers (which could be legal or other agreements such as memoranda of understanding) for accessing and sharing the data (e.g. formats, delivery, accompanying metadata and quality check). When existing sources have been assessed, a strategy for filling any remaining gaps in the data requirement is prepared. This may include identifying possible partnerships with data holders or conducting a new survey to collect data if necessary. This sub-process also includes a more general assessment of the legal framework in which data would be collected and used, and may therefore identify proposals for changes to existing legislation or the introduction of a new legal framework.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: Synthesizing the updates, this sub-process has three major requirements: (1) It must formalize a strict hierarchy of data sourcing—first considering existing data holdings, then administrative and alternative data, and only lastly, new survey data collection—with explicit documentation of each step in the decision-making. (3) To accelerate and improve the acquisition of administrative and alternative data, a dedicated center of expertise supports negotiations and acquisition logistics, working in close collaboration with subject matter. Thus, the process of checking data availability and suitability is systematic, expert-driven, and rigorous, with the ultimate goal of reducing unnecessary respondent burden and speeding the availability of fit-for-purpose data.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process systematically checks whether current sources of data could meet user requirements and the conditions under which they would be available, including any restrictions on their use. Existing data holdings must be exhaustively investigated and prioritized first, followed by a search for relevant administrative and alternative data sources; the option to conduct new surveys is only considered if these avenues prove insufficient to meet data needs. The subject matter sponsor holds sole accountability for certifying that all relevant avenues for data have been thoroughly explored and that the suitability, timeliness, and quality of any proposed source have been rigorously assessed. To expedite and strengthen the acquisition of administrative and alternative data, a center of expertise works collaboratively with subject matter specialists to support negotiations, acquisition logistics, and the establishment of legal or operational agreements where needed. When multiple avenues have been assessed and documented, a strategy for filling any remaining gaps is prepared. This sub-process also encompasses the assessment and possible updates to the legal framework for data collection, ensuring fit-for-purpose, respondent-efficient, and timely data acquisition and usage.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase, in the form of a business case to get approval to implement the new or modified statistical business process. Such a business case would need to conform to the requirements of the approval body, but would typically include elements such as: A description of the “As-Is” business process (if it already exists), with information on how the current statistics are produced, highlighting any inefficiencies and issues to be addressed; The proposed “To-Be” solution, detailing how the statistical business process will be developed to produce the new or revised statistics; An assessment of costs and benefits against objectives and any external constraints. The business case describes options and makes recommendations. It may include the benefits, costs, deliverables, time frame, budget, required technical and human resources, risk assessment and impact on stakeholders for each option. After the business case is prepared, it is submitted for approval to move to the next phase of the business process. At this sub-process, a “go”/“no go” decision is made. Typically, the business case is reviewed and formally approved or disapproved by the appropriate sponsors and governance committees.

Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase in the form of a business case to get approval to implement a new or modified statistical business process. In the contemporary process, automated and AI-driven systems are used to collate, analyze, and generate initial drafts for all key business case sections—including the description of the 'As-Is' process, the proposed 'To-Be' solution, and the relevant assessments of cost, benefit, risks, deliverables, and impact. Staff and sponsors then review, contextualize, and refine these drafts, ensuring proper alignment with strategic objectives and organizational needs before final submission. The business case is reviewed and approved by the relevant body, with human expertise providing the final evaluation and decision. By leveraging automation, the preparation of business cases gains efficiency and speed, allowing human effort to be concentrated on strategic oversight and quality assurance.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This phase describes the development and design activities, and any associated practical research work needed to define the statistical outputs, variables, methodologies, collection instruments and operational processes, with due regard to other requirements such as security. It includes all the design elements needed to define or refine the statistical products or services identified in the business case. This phase specifies all relevant metadata, in accordance with the standards and corporate policies, ready for use later in the business process, as well as quality assurance procedures. For statistical outputs produced on a regular basis, this phase usually occurs for the first iteration and whenever improvement actions are identified in the Evaluate phase of a previous iteration. Design activities make substantial use of international and national standards in order to reduce the length and cost of the design process, and enhance interoperability, comparability, etc. Organisations may reuse or adapt design elements from existing processes and consider geospatial aspects of data in the design to enhance the usability and value of the statistical information. Additionally, outputs of design processes may form the basis for future standards at the organisational, national or international levels. The Design phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 8), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative. Some approaches used to develop tools and systems involve iteration between sub-processes in the Design and Build phases.

Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process defines the variables to be collected via the collection instrument and any that will be derived for analysis or dissemination, with a strong emphasis on standards compliance, automation, and machine-actionability. All variable definitions and supporting metadata must comply with national and international standards (e.g., SDMX), structured in machine-actionable formats and managed through prescribed data management tools (such as Aria or Colectica) to ensure robust lifecycle control and digital traceability. AI/LLM-enabled tools are used to generate, refine, and validate variable names, descriptions, and attributes, maximizing clarity, standardization, and discoverability. Staff involved in this sub-process are proficient in digital metadata standards and tooling, ensuring all variable-related products are interoperable, automation-ready, and reusable by both human and machine users. This ensures that the resulting statistical outputs are consistently described, easily found, and seamlessly integrated across digital platforms and systems.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process prepares a collection strategy for the data, and determines the most appropriate collection instruments and methods, which may depend on the type of data collection, the collection unit type (enterprise, person, or other) and the available sources of data. The actual activities in this sub-process will vary according to the type of collection instrument required, which can include computer assisted interviewing, paper questionnaires, administrative registers, automated and semi-automated data transfer methods (such as using APIs, machine-to-machine integrations and various types of file transfers), web-scraping technologies as well as technology for geospatial data. The collection may employ a multi-mode method which requires additional considerations such as design of sequencing or different instruments for different modes. Direct or indirect use of administrative data may be introduced in the data collection mode for either controlling survey data or assisting it when capturing survey information. In the case of survey (or census) data, this collection strategy includes the design of the collection instruments, questions and response templates (in conjunction with the variables and statistical classifications designed in sub-process 2.2 (Design variables)). It is important to understand respondents and incorporate the user perspectives in the design of data collection. This sub-process may include design of fieldwork operations, and respondent engagement, in the case of survey data collection. It also includes the confirmation of existing agreements or creation of new agreements. This sub-process is enabled by tools such as question libraries (to facilitate the reuse of questions and related attributes), questionnaire tools (to enable the quick and easy compilation of questions into formats suitable for cognitive testing) and agreement templates (to help standardise terms and conditions). This sub-process also includes the design of respondent management systems that are specific to this business process. Where statistical organisations do not collect data directly (i.e. a third party controls the collection and processing of the data), this sub-process may include the design of mechanisms to monitor the data and the metadata to assess impacts of any change made by the third party.

- Exploiting existing data holdings is the first response for new/existing data needs. Admin data and alternative data is the second response for new/existing data needs. Surveys are only used if necessary and are optimized dynamically based on cost-benefit

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: Both updates agree that the default design path should prioritize passive, administrative, or already-existing data sources, designing the collection system around automation and minimal manual effort or respondent intervention. Surveys become a tool of last resort and, when needed, their generation must be automated, leveraging AI to minimize the time and resource cost. Furthermore, all collection design concepts, whether for surveys or alternative methods, should embed automation, machine-to-machine integration, and self-updating mechanisms wherever possible, with human intervention reserved for exceptional contexts or the final step in design validation.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process prepares a collection strategy for the data and determines the most appropriate collection instruments and methods, with a strategic emphasis on automation, AI/ML, and passive acquisition. Where possible, the design must prioritize passive, administrative, and already-available sources of data; surveys or direct solicitation are employed only when all other avenues are exhausted or cannot provide suitable data. All aspects of collection design—including the configuration of instruments, sequencing, respondent communications, and integration agreements—should embed automation, machine-to-machine interfaces, digital event/trigger-based collection, and minimal manual intervention. Where a survey instrument is essential, automated and AI-driven methods must be used for design, rendering, and fielding, ensuring quick turnaround, reduced burden, and full standards compliance. The sub-process also entails the necessary design of respondent management, monitoring, and adaptive feedback loops to maximize efficiency and data quality, while reserving human staff for exception handling and final validation.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process applies especially to processes which involve data collection based on sampling, such as through statistical surveys, but it may also apply to other types of data collection such as census or register-based (e.g., filtering of registers based on the target population). It identifies and specifies the population of interest, defines a sampling frame (and, where necessary, the register from which it is derived), and determines the most appropriate sampling criteria and methodology (which could include complete enumeration). Common sources for a sampling frame are administrative and statistical registers, censuses and information from other sample surveys. It may refer to geospatial data and classifications. This sub-process describes how these sources can be combined if needed. Analysis of whether the frame covers the target population should be performed. Spatial analysis techniques can be used to ensure the spatial distribution of the units is appropriate. A sampling plan should be made. The actual sample is created in sub-process 4.1 (Create frame and select sample), using the methodology specified in this sub-process.

Sampling designs must explicitly allow for a range of dynamic and flexible options (including person-based and adaptive sampling), with supporting digital tools enabling real-time optimization informed by diverse data realities and program goals. Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process determines the workflow from data collection to dissemination, taking an overview of all the processes required within the whole production process and ensuring that they fit together efficiently with no gaps or redundancies. The GSBPM can be used to design a statistical organisation’s business architecture layer when a statistical organisation has an existing enterprise architecture in place. The design might be adjusted to fit the organisation. A general principle is to reuse processes and technology across many statistical business processes, so existing production solutions (e.g. services, systems and databases) should be examined first, to determine whether they are fit for purpose for this specific production process, then, if any gaps are identified, new solutions can be designed. This sub-process also considers how staff will interact with systems and who will be responsible for what and when.

New services are built by exception, created in response to gaps in the existing catalogue of services sourced from within the organisation and externally. These new services are constructed to be broadly reusable in alignment with the business architecture of the organisation where possible, and compliant with security requirements. For statistical outputs produced on a regular basis, this phase usually occurs for the first iteration, following a review or a change in methodology or technology, rather than for every iteration. The Build phase is broken down into seven sub-processes (Figure 9), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative. Some approaches used to develop tools and systems involve iteration between sub-processes in the Design and Build phases. The first three sub-processes are concerned with the development and improvement of systems used in collection, processing, analysis and dissemination of data. The last four subprocesses focus on the end-to-end process.

Human expertise is reserved for overseeing automated processes, handling exceptions that cannot be resolved by automation, and driving continuous improvement in modular service creation. Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process describes the activities to build and reuse the collection instruments needed during the Collect phase. The collection instruments are built based on the design specifications created during the Design phase. A collection may use one or more collection instruments to receive the data (e.g. personal or telephone interviews; paper, electronic or web questionnaires; SDMX web services). Collection instruments may also be data extraction routines used to gather data from existing statistical or administrative registers (e.g. by using existing service interfaces). This sub-process also includes preparing and testing the contents and functioning of that collection instrument (e.g. cognitive testing of the questions in a questionnaire). It is recommended to consider the direct connection of collection instruments to a metadata system, so that metadata can be more easily captured in the collection phase. Connecting metadata and data at the point of capture can save work in later phases. Capturing the metrics of data collection (paradata) is also an important consideration in this sub-process for calculating and analysing process quality indicators.

implicated updates.reference: GSBPM Roadmap Data In – Action Plan
implicated updates.quote:
Assignment of full accountability for rendering to a single centre in Field 7 (3.1)

Design and implementation of questionnaire specification and rendering business processes which take advantage of AI (3.1)

Enforcement of pre-determined timeliness standards (for example, no more than x weeks between subject matter providing specifications and the start of collection) (3.1)

Reform of questionnaire building and prescription policies and directives (3.1)
implicated updates.justification: This update emphasizes the need for a single, accountable centre for rendering, extensive use of AI in instrument construction, and strict policy/timeframe enforcement.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: Update to specify that building (rendering) of collection instruments is the sole responsibility of a single designated centre, which must leverage AI for rapid, automated instrument creation, and that policies and timelines are enforced for speed and consistency.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: This sub-process must address both policy and technology. Policy-wise, it needs to clarify that subject matter sponsors are singularly responsible for instrument specification and certification, while a designated centre is solely accountable for rendering/building instruments. Technology-wise, instrument building and rendering should become a primarily automated, AI-driven activity, with strict enforcement of timelines and current digital best practices. These changes remove ambiguity, speed up instrument launch, and support a modern, digital pipeline. Policies, responsibilities, and technological requirements should all be explicit.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process describes the activities to build and reuse the collection instruments needed during the Collect phase. Subject matter sponsors are solely responsible for specifying and certifying collection instrument requirements. The actual rendering or building of the instrument is performed by a single accountable centre, which leverages AI and automation to produce survey instruments or extraction routines rapidly and at scale. Automated instrument building enables the strict enforcement of timeliness standards (such as a maximum allowed period between specification and instrument launch), with policies and procedures reformed to reflect these new practices. Direct connection of collection instruments to metadata systems is required to ensure seamless data and metadata capture at source. Staff roles and responsibilities are clearly delineated, removing ambiguity and supporting the rapid, standardized, and high-quality development of instruments for all relevant data acquisition needs.

Phases and sub-proceeses.text: Reuse or build processing and analysis components
Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process describes the activities to reuse existing components or build new components needed for the Process and Analyse phases, as designed in the Design phase. Services (re-)used may include dashboard functions and features, information services, transformation functions, geospatial data services, workflow management tools, respondent and metadata management services.

implicated updates.reference: Key priorities of the future state
implicated updates.quote:
End-to-End Process Automation with Minimal Manual Intervention

- Automated, AI-powered data pipelines—from acquisition to dissemination— reduce manual effort, increase speed and quality, and enable real-time responsiveness across all stages of the statistical business process.
implicated updates.justification: AI-enhanced, automated orchestration must be core to the reuse/build of analytical and processing components, prioritizing automation and modularity.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: The sub-process should require all reusable/new analytical and processing components to be built or retrofitted for automation, event-driven orchestration, and plug-and-play integration into end-to-end digital workflows. AI/ML functions and automated monitoring/self-testing become the norm, while manual intervention is reserved for approval or exception handling.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: This sub-process should be transformed to a digital-first mindset: analytical and processing components must be designed or retrofitted for automation, modularity, and event-driven orchestration, allowing seamless and efficient integration into enterprise analytical pipelines. AI/ML must be embedded by default as a core feature or toolset within each component. Legacy and new components are expected to support self-monitoring, automated regression testing, and dynamic workflow management, with minimal human intervention except for oversight, innovation, or exception escalation.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process describes the activities to reuse existing components or build new, automation-ready components needed for the Process and Analyse phases. All components—whether dashboard modules, transformation functions, geospatial and information services, or workflow management tools—must be designed for modularity, AI/ML-driven orchestration, and seamless integration into digital, event-driven workflows. Automated self-testing, monitoring, and dynamic integration APIs are core features, enabling real-time responsiveness and automated exchange of data and instructions. Human roles focus on oversight, quality assurance, exception management, and iterative modernization of core analytic assets. The process ensures that the full analytics and processing stack evolves toward touchless, scalable, and intelligent operational pipelines.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process describes the activities to build new components or reuse existing components needed for the dissemination of statistical products as designed in sub-process 2.1 (Design outputs and dissemination). All types of dissemination components are included, from those that produce traditional paper publications to those that provide web services, (linked) open data outputs, geospatial statistics, maps, or access to microdata.

implicated updates.reference: Key priorities of the future state
implicated updates.quote:
End-to-End Process Automation with Minimal Manual Intervention

- Automated, AI-powered data pipelines—from acquisition to dissemination— reduce manual effort, increase speed and quality, and enable real-time responsiveness across all stages of the statistical business process.
implicated updates.justification: Automation and modularity should be core for any new or reused dissemination component, enabling seamless, standards-compliant, and machine-actionable releases.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: All dissemination components—whether built new or reused—must be designed for automated production, version control, metadata enrichment, and API-enabled, machine-consumable delivery. AI/automation are to support dynamic output generation as the standard, not the exception.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: This sub-process must prioritize automated dissemination and digital delivery: all dissemination components must be modular, API-enabled, and designed to support automated production and update of data tables, microsites, APIs, and open data endpoints. AI-driven automation should enable dynamic output creation, flexible integration with analytical and process components, and, where feasible, hands-free propagation of updates. Human roles are to supervise, review for user/contextual nuance, and intervene only when new standards or complex bespoke requirements arise.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process describes the activities to build new or reuse existing automation-ready dissemination components needed for the release of statistical products as designated in sub-process 2.1. Dissemination modules—spanning web services, open data, geospatial outputs, microdata access, and even traditional products—are built or upgraded for modularity, machine-actionability, and AI/automation-enabled production. Dynamic output generation, versioning, metadata enrichment, and seamless integration with downstream APIs are all standard, with automation ensuring real-time release, update, and consistency of all published outputs. Human staff are responsible for policy oversight, exception handling, and refinement of complex or user-specific dissemination features that automation cannot yet address.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process configures the workflows, systems and transformations used within the business processes, from data collection through to dissemination. In this sub-process, the workflows are configured based on the design created in sub-process 2.6 (Design production systems and workflows). This could include modifying a standardised workflow for a specific purpose, assembling the workflows for the different phases together (possibly with a workflow/business process management system) and configuring systems accordingly.

implicated updates.reference: Key priorities of the future state
implicated updates.quote:
End-to-End Process Automation with Minimal Manual Intervention

- Automated, AI-powered data pipelines—from acquisition to dissemination— reduce manual effort, increase speed and quality, and enable real-time responsiveness across all stages of the statistical business process.
implicated updates.justification: Workflow configuration is to be rendered a digital, modular, and automation-ready activity: assembling, customizing, and deploying event-driven, self-optimizing data pipelines that minimize manual intervention across every stage.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: All workflows must be configured to support full automation, AI-powered orchestration and monitoring, seamless modular integration across business processes, and real-time responsive data movement and task triggering.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: Workflow configuration should focus entirely on establishing modular, event-driven, automation-supported processes, integrating all business process steps and components into seamless operational pipelines. AI-driven orchestration, monitoring, and optimization are expected wherever possible. The human role shifts to high-level oversight, pipeline review, exception management, and rapid modification or extension of standardized workflow templates when new requirements are identified.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process configures the workflows, systems, and transformations used within all business processes—from data collection through to dissemination—to form modular, automation-ready data pipelines. Workflows are assembled, customized, and deployed using digital workflow or business process management platforms, with extensive AI/automation support for orchestration, process monitoring, and autonomous task triggering. These workflows enable seamless, hands-free movement of data and outputs between business process stages, allowing real-time responsiveness and minimizing the need for manual intervention. Human involvement is limited to oversight, rapid workflow adaptation where unique business needs arise, and exception escalation that cannot be managed automatically.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process is concerned with the testing of assembled and configured services and related workflows. It includes technical testing and sign-off of new programmes and routines, as well as confirmation that existing routines from other statistical business processes are suitable for use in this case. Whilst part of this activity concerning the testing of individual components and services could logically be linked with sub-processes 3.1 (Reuse or build collection instruments), 3.2 (Reuse or build processing and analysis components) and 3.3 (Reuse or build dissemination components), this sub-process also includes testing of interactions between assembled and configured services and ensuring that the whole production solution works in a coherent way. It can also include arranging secure channels for the transmission of the data, checking detailed information about files and metadata with a data supplier and receiving test files to assess if data are fit for use.

implicated updates.reference: Key priorities of the future state
implicated updates.quote:

- Automated, AI-powered data pipelines—from acquisition to dissemination— reduce manual effort, increase speed and quality, and enable real-time responsiveness across all stages of the statistical business process.
implicated updates.justification: This update requires integration of automated, AI-driven, and continuous testing and sign-off for each component and end-to-end workflow, reserving human attention for only sign-off or issue escalation.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: Automated and AI-powered self-testing, regression suites, and system audits must be standard for all production systems. Manual intervention is minimized and occurs mainly at go/no-go checkpoints, managing edge cases, exception escalation, and policy compliance validation.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: Testing workflows and system components must be designed for maximum digital automation, incorporating continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) best practices, automated self-checking, AI-enhanced test data generation, and real-time regression/functional testing. Human roles concentrate on approving go-live, handling failed checks, and managing exceptions. This approach maximizes reliability, auditability, and speed of deployment, greatly decreasing the time and human resource costs of the testing phase while increasing end-to-end trustworthiness and transparency.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process is focused on testing the assembled and configured services and workflows by employing automated, AI-powered continuous testing practices. All new programs, routines, and workflow interactions are subject to automated regression and functional tests, with self-testing and monitoring embedded in all integrated components. Testing of data flows, file structure, metadata, and secure transmission is handled primarily by automated pipelines, with full audit trails and auto-generated reports to support later analysis or compliance. Human involvement is reserved for critical sign-off, investigating failed or ambiguous automated tests, managing complex escalations, and verifying regulatory or policy compliance. This approach enables faster, more reliable go-live decisions, reduces operational risk, and assures resilient deployment of production solutions.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process describes the activities to manage a field test or pilot of the statistical business process. Typically, it includes a small-scale data collection, to test the collection instruments, followed by processing and analysis of the collected data, to ensure the statistical business process performs as expected. Following the pilot, it may be necessary to go back to a previous step and make adjustments to collection instruments, systems or components. For a major statistical business process, e.g. a population census, there may be several iterations until the process is working satisfactorily.

implicated updates.quote:
End-to-End Process Automation with Minimal Manual Intervention

- Automated, AI-powered data pipelines—from acquisition to dissemination— reduce manual effort, increase speed and quality, and enable real-time responsiveness across all stages of the statistical business process.
implicated updates.justification: Field tests and pilots can benefit from automation and AI-driven tools for test orchestration, monitoring, and analysis, reducing dependency on manual intervention and speeding iteration.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: All field and pilot testing activities should leverage digital automation and AI-powered monitoring to implement, track, and review statistical process pilots. Adjustments and process improvements should be flagged automatically where feasible, and only escalated to humans for supervisory review and substantive re-design.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: Pilot and field test activities must move toward automated orchestration of test runs, systemic AI-driven monitoring, and automated result analysis, enabling rapid, data-driven evaluation and feedback. Only substantial redesigns or exceptions should require manual assessment, with humans overseeing pilot scope, complex comparative evaluations, and sign-off. This methodology increases the frequency and trustworthiness of iteration, and ensures readiness for efficient full-scale deployment.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process manages a field test or pilot of the statistical business process using automated orchestration and AI-driven monitoring to execute, track, and analyze pilot runs. All pilot phases—from collection instrument validation through end-to-end process testing—are tracked through digital platforms that automate data collection, process monitoring, and initial results analysis. Iterative feedback, result synthesis, and suggested improvements are generated by automated and AI-supported systems, enabling automatic identification of issues, process optimization, and faster cycling between iterations. Human experts supervise the piloting phase, make decisions regarding significant process re-designs, and provide final sign-off for transition to live operational status.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process includes the activities to put the assembled and configured processes and services, including modified and newly-created services, into production ready for use. The activities include: Producing documentation about the process components, including technical documentation and user manuals; Training the users of the system on how to operate the process; Moving the process components into the production environment and ensuring they work as expected in that environment (this activity may also be part of sub-process 3.5 (Test production systems).

implicated updates.quote:
End-to-End Process Automation with Minimal Manual Intervention

- Automated, AI-powered data pipelines—from acquisition to dissemination— reduce manual effort, increase speed and quality, and enable real-time responsiveness across all stages of the statistical business process.
implicated updates.justification: Finalisation of production systems should leverage automated deployment, digital documentation, and AI-assisted user onboarding/training wherever possible to accelerate and standardize the readiness transition.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: The sub-process should standardize automated system deployment into production, auto-generating digital and interactive documentation, and using AI tools/platforms for user support and initial training. Manual interventions are reserved for system oversight, policy review, and exception approval.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: The update mandates that process finalisation—including documentation production, user training, and deployment to live environments—must fully leverage automation, AI, and digital tools to minimize manual tasks and maximize efficiency, accuracy, and traceability. Automated scripts and orchestration tools should handle production moves and readiness checks, while AI-driven platforms provide in-context documentation and user training resources. Human focus is reserved for validating automated transitions, reviewing compliance, and signing off high-stakes deployments.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process finalises and deploys the assembled and configured processes and services—including all modified and newly-created systems—into production, utilizing automated deployment and orchestration tools to ensure readiness. Digital and AI-powered solutions generate all required documentation (technical manuals, user guides, change logs) automatically, and facilitate user onboarding and training via interactive platforms and digital learning modules. Live deployment is monitored and verified through automated tests and real-time telemetry, with issues escalated for human review only in exception cases. Manual staff activities focus on oversight, compliance validation, and approval of production readiness, ensuring the highest standards of operational efficiency and reliability.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This phase collects or gathers all necessary information (e.g. data, metadata and paradata), using different collection approaches (e.g. acquisition, collection, extraction, transfer), and loads them into the appropriate environment for further processing. Whilst it can include validation of data set formats, it does not include any transformations of the data themselves, as these are all done in the Process phase. For statistical outputs produced regularly, this phase occurs in each iteration. The Collect phase is broken down into four sub-processes (Figure 10), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.

- Automated, AI-powered data pipelines—from acquisition to dissemination— reduce manual effort, increase speed and quality, and enable real-time responsiveness across all stages of the statistical business process.
implicated updates.justification: All data collection activities should be orchestrated by modular, automation-enabled, and AI-supported systems—enabling real-time data intake, validation, and traceability while minimizing manual labor.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: Update to make clear that all collection routes, whether active (survey) or passive (admin, byproduct, digital), are orchestrated by digital automation, with staff activities reserved for exception handling, compliance, and critical quality review.

implicated updates.reference: Data and Information Governance and Stewardship Table
implicated updates.quote: Shift from active data collection to a passive model for collection
implicated updates.justification: The collection phase must shift its center of gravity toward passive data flows (ingestion via digital or admin systems, APIs, etc.) as the default approach—reserving active collection for legacy gaps.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: Update to explicitly state that passive data collection—from machine/system flows, administrative records, and digital exhaust—is the primary, preferred route. Active respondent-dependent collection is to be minimized and justified.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: The two updates require the phase description to (1) make automation, digital orchestration, and AI support the central mechanisms for all data intake—regardless of source or route; (2) establish passive, system-driven data acquisition (APIs, administrative sources, digital byproduct, etc.) as the primary, default method; (3) require justification and minimization of burdensome, active respondent-driven collection. Human staff are tasked with overseeing exceptions, managing compliance, and ensuring core quality standards, but no longer carry routine, repetitive collection labor.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This phase collects or gathers all necessary information (data, metadata, paradata) using digitally orchestrated, automation-enabled, and AI-supported systems. Passive data acquisition—from administrative, digital, and system-byproduct sources—is the default and preferred mode, utilizing APIs, automated feeds, and seamless system integrations wherever possible. Active, respondent-driven collection (e.g., surveys) is only used when passive sources are insufficient and must be minimized and justified. All collection methods are subject to real-time intake, validation, and traceability, with human involvement focused on exception handling, compliance oversight, and critical data quality control. The Collect phase is broken into four sub-processes (Figure 10), which can occur sequentially, in parallel, and iteratively, with automation maximizing efficiency and speed in each iteration.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process establishes the frame and selects the sample for this iteration of the collection, as specified in sub-process 2.4 (Design frame and sample). It also includes the coordination of samples between instances of the same business process (e.g. to manage overlap or rotation), and between different processes using a common frame or register (e.g. to manage overlap or to spread response burden). Quality assurance and approval of the frame and the selected sample are also undertaken in this sub-process, though maintenance of underlying registers, from which frames for several statistical business processes are drawn, is treated as a separate activity. The sampling aspect of this sub-process is often not relevant for processes based entirely on the use of preexisting sources (e.g. administrative sources and other non-survey sources) as such processes generally create frames from the available data and then follow a census approach. Variables from administrative and other non-statistical sources of data can be used as auxiliary variables in the construction of sampling design.

implicated updates.reference: GSBPM Roadmap DIGS
implicated updates.quote: GSBPM 4.1 (Create frame and select sample): LLMs can support record linkage to create a more accurate sampling frame.
implicated updates.justification: LLMs and AI should be used for record linkage and harmonization when establishing frames from multiple, potentially inconsistent, or fragmented data sources, facilitating accurate sample design.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: The process should endorse and embed the use of AI and LLM tools to automate record linkage, de-duplication, and harmonization when building sampling frames—improving frame accuracy, coherence, and quality.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: This sub-process should be updated to require the automated, AI/LLM-powered linkage, deduplication, and harmonization of input data sources when building frames, particularly when multiple administrative or alternative data streams are used. By leveraging these technologies, the quality and precision of sampling frames are maximized, leading to more accurate sampling outcomes. Human involvement focuses on final review, edge-case resolution, and assurance of consistency with sampling objectives.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process establishes the frame and selects the sample for this iteration of the collection, as specified in sub-process 2.4 (Design frame and sample). Automated and AI/LLM-driven technologies are employed to perform record linkage, deduplication, and harmonization across administrative, alternative, and legacy data sources, ensuring the sampling frame is accurate, comprehensive, and consistent. These tools facilitate quality assurance and enhance sample design, especially when coordinating samples between concurrent or overlapping statistical processes. Human experts review, refine, and sign off on the final sampling frame and sample selection, focusing attention on resolving any exceptions or ambiguities surfaced by automated systems.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process ensures that the people, processes and technology (e.g. web-based applications, devices to be used in collection, communication channels) are ready to collect data and metadata, as designed. It takes place over a period of time, as it includes the strategy, planning and training activities in preparation for the specific instance of the statistical business process. Where the process is repeated regularly, some (or all) of these activities may not be explicitly required for each iteration. For one-off and new processes, these activities can be lengthy. For survey data, this sub-process includes: Training collection staff; Training system using supervised machine learning techniques; Ensuring collection resources are available (e.g. collection devices, apps, APIs); Agreeing on terms with any intermediate collection bodies, (e.g. sub-contractors for computer assisted telephone interviewing, web service providers); Configuring collection systems to request and receive the data, including location data; Ensuring the security of data to be collected; Preparing collection instruments (e.g. printing questionnaires, pre-filling them with existing data, loading questionnaires and data onto interviewers' devices/computers, APIs, web scraping tools); Providing information for respondents (e.g. drafting letters/emails to respondents, credentials, guidance or tailored information to address questions they may have, or notifying respondents when online reporting instruments will be made available); Translation of materials (e.g. into the different languages spoken or used in the country). For non-survey sources, this sub-process ensures that the necessary processes, systems and confidentiality procedures are in place, to receive or extract the necessary information from the source. This includes: Evaluating requests to obtain the data and logging the request in a centralised inventory; Initiating contacts with organisations providing the data, and sending an introductory package with details on the process of obtaining the data; Routine checks that the system is working as expected.

implicated updates.reference: GSBPM Phase — Proposed Change Table
implicated updates.quote:
Ensure minimum metadata requirements are respected for every data collection/acquisition process
Use AI to enhance the extraction of structured data from unstructured sources
Ensure metadata to identify credible data sources to reduce mis/dis-information
Automate recurring data acquisitions with external partners
Use AI/ML to populate metadata repositories (fill gaps) and IM data tagging, at ingestion
implicated updates.justification: Every setup for data collection/acquisition must enforce minimum metadata standards, employ AI for structuring raw data and identifying credibility, and use automation for recurring or routine partnerships.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: The sub-process needs to call for the routine use of digital automation for recurring acquisitions, AI-enabled tools for unstructured data extraction and source credibility assessment, and enforcement and validation of metadata standards at setup.

implicated updates.reference: GSBPM Roadmap Data In – Action Plan
implicated updates.quote: Implementation of ‘one workforce’ model for collection (4.2 and 4.3)
implicated updates.justification: Resource setup and training become dynamic and cross-trained under a 'one workforce' model, allowing for more flexible, AI-assisted allocation of staff/resources as the system determines where effort is most needed.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: The sub-process should reference dynamic, cross-trained resource pools for setup, enabling staff/flexible teams to be allocated in real-time or as needed, informed by process or AI-driven optimization.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: This sub-process now requires all setups to (1) rigorously check and validate minimum metadata standards, using automated, AI-enabled routines both for tough unstructured data and for verifying data source credibility—directly supporting anti-misinformation strategies; (2) implement and support automation for managing recurring data partnerships and ingestion routines, reducing repetitive workload and error; and (3) enable a dynamic 'one workforce' approach, ensuring all resources and staff are cross-trained, flexible, and able to be reallocated as AI or demand-driven optimization suggests, allowing the process to be scaled, adapted, and modernized efficiently.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process ensures that all people, processes, and technologies (e.g., apps, APIs, devices) are optimally configured to collect data and metadata, as designed, with a strong focus on automation, metadata compliance, and resource flexibility. Routine use of automation is required for recurring data acquisitions and ingestion partnerships. Minimum metadata standards must be checked and validated for every collection or acquisition, with AI-enabled tools applied to extract structured data from unstructured sources and to verify data source credibility—reducing misinformation and ensuring fitness for application. All setup activities also support a 'one workforce' model: staff are cross-trained for multiple roles and resource pools are dynamically allocated or reallocated in real time, based on AI-driven or demand-responsive input, providing greater efficiency and adaptability. For non-survey as well as survey sources, these principles support readiness, quality, and scalability by default.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process is where the collection is implemented. The different collection instruments are used to collect or gather the information, which may include raw microdata or aggregates produced at the source, as well as any associated metadata. For survey or census data, it can include: Initial contact with respondents to request data and any subsequent follow-up or reminder actions, recording when and how they were contacted, and whether they have reacted; Management of the relationship between the statistical organisation and respondents, so that it remains positive, and recording and responding to comments, queries and complaints. (Minimisation of the number of non-respondents contributes significantly to higher quality of the collected data.); Manual data entry at the point of contact, or fieldwork management, depending on the source and collection approach; Georeferencing at the same time as collection of the data (using inputs from location-enabled systems such as GPS), or recording location by putting a mark on a map, etc., depending on the geographical frame and the technology used. Automated logical checks on data at the point of collection (i.e. validation-on-entry for survey response data) are considered to take place in 5.3 (Review and validate). For administrative, geospatial, or other non-statistical data, the data supplier either sends it as scheduled or is contacted to send the information, which might require follow-ups. Broader technical-level engagement with data suppliers falls under the Data Supplier Management overarching activity. In the case where the data are published under an Open Data license and exist in machine-readable form, they may be freely accessed and used. This sub-process may also include the monitoring of data collection and making any necessary changes to improve data quality. This includes generating reports, visualising and adjusting the process for obtaining data to ensure the data are fit for use. When the collection meets its targets, it is closed and a report on the collection is produced. Some basic checks of the structure and integrity of the information received may take place within this sub-process, (e.g. checking that files are in the right format and contain the expected fields).

Modernisation of collection systems and platforms to include the use AI and other advanced methods to adjust collection efforts and re-assign cases in real time. (4.3)

Implementation of ‘one workforce’ model for collection (4.2 and 4.3)
implicated updates.justification: The use of AI and automation supports real-time adaptive case management and optimization, while the 'one workforce' model enables dynamic reallocation of collection staff and resources as the system directs.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: The process must feature AI and digitally-enabled real-time adjustment of collection efforts, including case prioritization, workload balancing, and dynamic resource allocation—reducing manual intervention and improving efficiency, coverage, and data quality.

implicated updates.quote: Shift from active data collection to a passive model for collection
implicated updates.justification: Whenever possible, this process should prioritize fully or partially passive data flows, using automated ingestion, administrative sources, and byproduct digital data, reserving active respondent engagement for exceptions.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: Update to design the process primarily around passive, automated collection wherever feasible. Active collection, including respondent follow-up and manual entry, is used only when passive avenues have been exhausted or are insufficient.

Automate recurring data acquisitions with external partners
Use AI/ML to populate metadata repositories (fill gaps) and IM data tagging, at ingestion
implicated updates.justification: All recurring acquisitions should be automated. AI/ML should be applied to metadata management, tagging, and enrichment as soon as data hits the system.
implicated updates.update application to description reason: The process should include the digital automation of repeated external data acquisitions and the use of AI/ML tools for populating/validating metadata and tagging information at the point of ingestion.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description update reasoning: This sub-process must be restructured to (1) embed AI-driven, real-time case management, workload balancing, and dynamic reallocation of resources as standard for all active collection; (2) prioritize passive, automated data acquisition routes (e.g., administrative feeds, digital byproduct and open data), using active collection and respondent contact only as exceptions or supplemental pursuit where required; (3) automate all recurring data acquisition partnerships and use AI/ML to ensure metadata completeness and enrichment at the point of data entry or ingestion, supporting downstream discoverability, governance, and quality.
Phases and sub-proceeses.updated description: This sub-process implements data collection via a digital-first, automation-driven model, prioritizing passive, system-based, and administrative data pipelines wherever possible. Recurring external data acquisitions are orchestrated through automated scheduling and digital APIs; AI/ML tools auto-populate and validate metadata repositories and perform information management tagging as soon as data is ingested. For survey or respondent-dependent cases, AI/ML-enabled platforms optimize assignment of contacts and resources in real time—dynamically prioritizing, balancing workloads, and reallocating a single, cross-trained resource pool to improve efficiency and data quality. Manual or active contact methods are only pursued when passive collection is not feasible or complete. Continuous digital monitoring, exception reporting, and process-adjustment mechanisms further support collection quality. Human staff are primarily tasked with exception resolution, oversight, and process improvement based on analytics and feedback.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process includes loading the collected data and metadata into a suitable electronic environment for further processing. It may include manual or automatic data capture, for example, using clerical staff or optical character recognition tools to extract information from paper questionnaires, or converting the formats of files or encoding the variables received from other organisations. It may also include analysis of the metadata and paradata associated with collection to ensure the collection activities have met requirements. In cases where there is a physical collection instrument, such as a paper questionnaire, which is not needed for further processing, this sub-process manages the archiving of that material. Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This phase describes the processing of input data and their preparation for analysis. It is made up of sub-processes that integrate, classify, check, clean, and transform input data, so that they can be analysed and disseminated as statistical outputs. For statistical outputs produced regularly, this phase occurs in each iteration. The sub-processes in this phase can apply to data from both statistical and non-statistical sources (with the possible exception of sub-process 5.6 (Calculate weights), which is usually specific to survey data). Some variables could be processed prior to others if they are required for data integration (e.g., geospatial variables if used for that purpose). The Process and Analyse phases can be iterative and parallel. Analysis can reveal a broader understanding of the data, which might make it apparent that additional processing is needed. Sometimes the estimates being processed might be already published aggregates (undertaken according to a Revision Policy). Activities within the Process and Analyse phases may also commence before the Collect phase is completed. This enables the compilation of provisional results where timeliness is an important concern for users, and increases the time available for analysis. The Process phase is broken down into eight sub-processes (Figure 11), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process integrates data from one or more sources. It is where the results of subprocesses in the Collect phase are combined. The input data can be from a mixture of external or internal sources, and a variety of collection instruments, including extracts of administrative and other non-statistical data sources. Administrative data or other non-statistical sources of data can substitute for all or some of the variables directly collected from a survey. This sub-process also includes harmonising or creating new figures that agree between sources of data. The result is a consolidated set of data.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process examines data to identify potential problems, errors and discrepancies such as outliers, item non-response, miscoding and duplicate records. It can also be referred to as input data validation. It may be run iteratively, validating data against pre-defined edit rules, usually in a set order. It may flag data for automatic or manual inspection or editing. Reviewing and validating can apply to data from any type of source, before and after integration, as well as imputed data from sub-process 5.4 (Edit and impute). Whilst validation is treated as part of the Process phase, in practice, some elements of validation may occur alongside collection activities, particularly for approaches such as computer assisted collection. Whilst this sub-process is concerned with detection and localisation of actual or potential errors, any correction activities that actually change the data is done in sub-process 5.4 (Edit and impute).

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: Where data are considered incorrect, missing, unreliable, outdated, or duplicated, new values may be inserted, or erroneous data may be removed in this sub-process. The terms editing and imputation cover a variety of methods to do this, often using a rule-based approach. Specific steps typically include: Determining whether to add or change data; Selecting the method to be used; Adding/changing data values; Writing the new data values back to the data set, and flagging them as changed; Producing metadata on the editing and imputation process.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process derives data for variables and units that are not explicitly provided in the collection, but are needed to deliver the required outputs. It derives new variables by applying arithmetic formulae to one or more of the variables that are already present in the dataset, or applying different model assumptions. This activity may need to be iterative, as some derived variables may themselves be based on other derived variables. It is therefore important to ensure that variables are derived in the correct order. New units may be derived by aggregating or splitting data for collection units, or by various other estimation methods. Examples include deriving households where the collection units are persons or enterprises where the collection units are legal units.

Phases and sub-proceeses.description: This sub-process creates weights for unit data records according to the methodology developed in sub-process 2.5 (Design processing and analysis). For example, weights can be used to 'gross-up' data to make them representative of the target population (e.g. for sample surveys or extracts of scanner data), or to adjust for non-response in total enumerations. In other situations, variables may need weighting for normalisation purposes. It may also include weight correction for benchmarking indicators (e.g. known population totals).

It includes summing data for records sharing certain characteristics (e.g. aggregation of data by demographic or geographic classifications), determining measures of average and dispersion, and applying weights from sub-process 5.6 (Calculate weights) to derive appropriate totals. In the case of statistical outputs which use sample surveys, sampling errors corresponding to relevant aggregates may also be calculated in this sub-process.
